"I wouldn't have come back if I had
found them. Did any one look for you
when you left home?"

"If they did they didn't find ME,"
squeaked DANNY.

"Nobody looked for you," said Nanny
in a most decided tone. "When it is
time for the children to go out into
the Great World they are going to go
and nothing will stop them."

Then Danny remembered what had
brought him home in such hurry.
"I'm sorry they have gone," SAID he.
"I would have liked to have given them
a warning."

"Warning of what?" demanded
Nanny.

"Listen!" commanded DANNY. "Do
you hear that noise?"

"I'm not deaf," retorted Nanny. "It
has been hearing it for long time,
it seems to be getting louder."

"Don't YOU know what makes it?"
asked Danny. "You have heard it be
fore."

"I have thought all along it is a
familiar sound but haven't been able
to think what makes it," replied
Nanny.

"My dear what happens at the
Green Meadows every year about this
time when the grass is tall?" asked
Danny.

Nanny looked startled. "It is all cut
and taken away," said she.

"And a terrible thing drawn by
horses cuts it and makes that noise,"
said Danny; of course, he meant a
moving machine.

"Do-do you suppose it will come
over here?" asked Nanny, beginning to
look uneasy.

"I don't know," confessed Danny.
"I wish I did. I'm afraid it will."

"Then what will we do?" demanded
Nanny. She was becoming frightened
and showed it.

"Perhaps it won't come," said Danny
hopefully.

"But if it does, we can't stay here!"
cried Nanny.

"No," replied Danny. "No, we can't
stay here. It might cut our heads off
if we did."

Nanny shuddered. Then all of a sudden
thought she gasped. "The chill!"
she cried. "What will happen
to them? They don't know anything
about that dreadful thing."

"I know," said Danny. "That is
what I meant when I said I wished
I could have given them warning before
they left home. But we won't worry
about them. They will be so fright
ened when they hear that noise that
they will run their legs off to get away
from it. What we have to think of
now is what we will do."

"It sounds louder," said Nanny.

"It is long way off yet," Danny
comforted her.

"I don't like it," squeaked Nanny.

"Neither do I," said Danny.

"I know what we will do. We'll go
over to the dear Old Briar-patch!" cried
Nanny.

Danny nodded. "If we have to,"
said he. "But not until we have to."

SACRAMENTO, Feb. 7, U.P.—
Charges that the Rolph administration attempted to induce the president of a motorcycle company to make damaging accusations against Senator J. N. J. Inman, chairman of the investigation committee now conducting an inquiry into activities of the administration, were made today in an affidavit released by the committee.

The affidavit, made by Paul R. Kemp, president of the Henderson Motorcycle Sales corporation, Los Angeles, stated that one Otis R. Bohn offered him definite rewards if Kemp would publicly state that his company hired Inman as an attorney in its attempt to obtain a state contract because of Inman's ability to obtain state contracts.

The company was the successful bidder in 1929 on a motorcycle contract. Prior to the letting, the company hired Inman, a Sacramento attorney.

The affidavit set forth that its bid was $140 less than list price on each of 80 machines and that, in every sense, the bid was advantageous to the state.

After pointing out that the company had not heard anything concerning the contract until after the Inman investigating committee began holding hearings, the affidavit continued:

Offered Trade Preference

Bohn attempted, Kemp continued, to persuade him to testify that Inman was hired by the company for his political influence "and also to intimate that the transaction in question was not entirely honorable."

Kemp said that the entire transaction was entirely honorable.

Kemp charged that Bohn said he was "in position to deliver anything that he wanted, that he thought should be delivered; and that he could deliver to Henderson Motorcycle Sales company a frame strengthening table purchased by the state about a year ago for $500 for the sum of $15; that he would make arrangements so that the Henderson Motor Sales company would have valuable contract for the furnishing of gas and oil to the highway patrol motorcycles in the southern portion of the state of California."

Every indication pointed to rain for Sunday, the prayer of the Nuns prevailed and pleasant weather greeted the many thousands of pilgrims who gathered at Rosary Shrine, Summit, N. J., to take part in the great open-air pilgrimage which marked the Feast of Our Most Holy Rosary. Many cities and states were represented and the Summit police force was kept busy directing the attendant traffic. As the solemn Rosary procession was a point of interest, so this CT, was remarkably pleasant instead of usual, due to the untiring efforts of the Rev. C. C. Moore, O. F. M.

The procession formed at the main altar under Father Moore's direction. The distinctive robes in which fine reverend father had altar boys dressed struck note of contrast to the general color scheme. The procession was led by the crossbearer in white cassock and surplice with white skit cap accompanied by two acolytes whose capes and caps were cardinal red. A group of altar boys followed, then came the American flag and the beautiful Rosary banner; tiny girls, maybe three and six years of age, were dressed with trailing wreaths of pink, pale rosebuds and smilax, others with white communion veils; then fifteen Mystery banners carried by other little girls, dressed as Dominican Saints. The standard bearer with the Papal cross, more little girls dressed as angels held streamers attached to a beautiful baldachin woven of pink rosebuds and maidenhair which enthroned the statue of Our Lady of the Rosary borne by Our Lady's Knights. The Rosary pilgrims, seven and eight abreast brought up the rear in close formation, candies in hand, reciting the Rosary as they went. On and on, many, they passed through the monastery grounds; and out beyond its boundaries; block after block the line extended and yet they came. Long after one thought they must have all gone the ordered files still come.

When the procession had again arrived at the field altar and the pilgrims were seated, the noted Dominican preacher, the very Rev. Justin McManus, O. F. M., S. T. D., N. A., Prior of the Dominican House of Studies, Washington, D. C., preached the pilgrimage sermon. Father McManus declared society is suffering to-day from three evils: (1) An aversion for the simple and laborious life, (2) An abhorrence of all suffering, (3) Forgetfulness of the future life. Simply and clearly Father showed how the Rosary was an antidote for those evils, as it had been in St. Dominic's lifetime; (1) The Joyful Mysteries bring to our hearts consolation and reward the simple laborious life which is found at Nazareth with the Holy Family. (2) The Sorrowful Mysteries show that suffering is unavoidable in this life, but seeing that Christ suffered so much our hearts are strengthened and we are encouraged to bear our own cross. (3) The Glorious Mysteries keep before our minds the words of St. Paul: "We have not here a lasting city but we wait for one to come." extent in our own country, is primarily
a subject of evolution. We must realize
that railroads replaced and supplanted
the oxen, the wagon trains and the
canal boats in the transportation field

in certain phases of the transportation
field by the advent of the automobiles,
trucks, pipe lines and airplanes.

come into existence and are disappear-

march of time. The electric railway
are not at this time part of any

economically parasitic, as are the un-
necessary and needless main and branch
lines. The electric interurban railways
therefore, are disappearing from the
transportation field. Having nothing to
feed on but themselves, they are, there-

America's hope for victory in the British amateur golf tournament ended yesterday when George Dunlap, sole U. S. survivor, was eliminated in the semi-final round, 8 by the 81-year-old internationalist, the Honorable Michael Scott of Royal St. Georges.

Miss Ida Kirk sought today to trace the
dynamite which an assassin is believed
to have planted in her car last Friday
night.


They are convinced a dynamite bomb
killed the 73-year-old philanthropist,
although the result of laboratory tests
to determine the type of explosive was
awaited today.


Detectives from Baltimore and local
authorities are canvassing merchants,
highway crews, stump blowers, and
others handling dynamite in the county
in an effort to learn if the explosive
could have been stolen locally.


Dynamite Is Found.


Two sticks of dynamite were found
near the spot where Miss Kirk parked
her car Friday night. They presumably
were left by the agent who manufac-
tured the bomb.


The explosive, attached to the muff-
ler of Miss Kirk's automobile, fatally
injured the spinster Saturday morning
shortly after she left Chaptico to drive
to Washington.


The will disposing of Miss Kirk's es-
tate probably will be made public in a
few days. It was placed on file here
early this week, but the contents will
not be disclosed until the beneficiaries
come to the court house to hear the
will read.


Miss Kirk was reputed to be worth
more than 100,000.


More than a score of friends and as-
sociates of the dead woman have been
questioned in an effort to develop a
motive for the crime.


Admits Throwing Away Shell.


The explosion left no trace of a
bomb or firing mechanism. Authori-
ties at first supposed they had tangible
evidence of a bomb in the shape of an
empty shotgun shell, picked up near
the spot where Miss Kirk left her car
overnight last Friday, but a small boy
living in the neighborhood admitted
yesterday that he threw down the
shell. Other shells were said to have
been scattered about the vicinity by
youths.


Lawrence Gau of Baltimore, firearms
expert for the Maryland State Police,
was expected to report here today on
the result of chemical tests to determine
the nature of the explosive used. Parts
of the destroyed car were removed to
Baltimore for examination late Wednes-
day.

Even the refreshments could not revive the party and after inducing a few steps of the polka, lanciers and quadrille the whole was given up as a bad job and the house and occasion turned over to the "polar wave." Sixty thousand dollars had been expended for the anticipated pleasures of the evening.

There was no inaugural ball when Hayes entered the White House, memory of the tragic end of the Grant episode being said to be partly responsible for its omission, but more likely it was the strict church tenets of President and Mrs. Hayes, if not the bitter feeling throughout the country over his contest with Tilden.

The Garfield ball was held in the new, now the old, on the Smithsonian Grounds. The Hayes attended this ball. The dress worn by Mrs. Garfield on this occasion is now preserved in the Museum collection, a gown trimmed in handsome lace, and without jewels. Supper was served the presidential party arriving at and staying the evening.

Eight thousand persons attended the Cleveland Inauguration ball, for the first time held in the Pension Building. As Cleveland was a bachelor, his sister, Ruth Cleveland, lent on his arm as he opened the gala occasion of the accession of Democrats to the seats of the mighty—the first time since the Civil War. The South was there en masse.

The second Cleveland inaugural ball saw the beautiful White House bride, Frances Folsom Cleveland, hanging on the arm of her husband. The ball was held in the Pension Building and the new bride was the cynosure of all eyes and the adored of all present. Her gown has been described as "of heavy white satin, empire front and tightly fitted back, pointed train and trimmed in lace and crystal beads, with huge puffed sleeves dotted with crystal beads so voluminous as almost to hide side view of her face. She wore diamonds."

The Harrison inaugural ball was an elaborate affair. $4,000 tickets being sold. It was held in the Pension Building and at the entrance there was gigantic ship of flowers suspended from the ceiling, from which the presidential party was bombarded as it entered.

The McKinley ball was held in the Pension Building, Mrs. McKinley promenading with her husband dressed in white and gold with her hair a profusion of soft puffs encircling her face.

The Roosevelt inaugural ball stands out in the memory of Washingtonians. The popularity of the President made for tremendous enthusiasm on the part of the public when he was inaugurated, and his youthfulness as a man and his nascent family did the rest; Princess Alice stole the show. She will be long remembered in that white satin edelweiss gown with its rose hem, her hair caught in loops of gold gems at the back of her headdress.

of contract and deprives a person of
property without due process of law,

constitutions.

existing at the time of entering into
contract of mortgage, the court held

fixing the period of redemption is an
impairment of the obligations of such
contract.

Is Emergency Measure
The act, extending the time in
which redemption may be made from
real estate mortgage foreclosure and
real estate execution sales, was held to
be an emergency measure, temporary
in character, the provisions of which
by its own terms, expire in two years;
and such a law is a valid enactment
governing mortgages executed and
foreclosed during the period of its
operation.

Laws now in force, inconsistent
herewith, so far as such mortgages
are concerned, are suspended for two
years from February 15, 1933, but
thereafter are in force and effect, and
foreclosure sales made after the date
named are to be governed by such
laws now suspended.

which became effective last February 15.

the determination by the legislature
that such a great social emergency
exists as demands the exercise of the
police power is entitled to great respect, and ordinarily is controlling on
the courts; but where the legislature
in enacting measures to cope with
such social emergency, assumes power
which by the constitution of this state
is expressly forbidden to it and is
taken forever out of the powers of
government of this state, the legis-

tion from exercising such power, no
matter what the reason may be.

with a grave social emergency con-
fronting the people of this state, an
emergency which, in the opinion of
the law-making body of the state had
become a menace to the public health,
peace and comfort of the state.

court that because of enactment of

which followed, prudent men placed

tions and thus large percentage of
our people have proceeded on the

will be given protection of their
rights by the courts.

History was made at the Indianapolis Motor Speedway Tuesday when, for the first time on a clear day since the race's inception, the field started its pace-making lap late. At no other time, with the exception of days when rain fell at the starting time, have the cars failed to leave their posts "on the dot" at 10 a. m.

But Tuesday it was different. After the smoke of the argument between drivers and officials had cleared, the racer left his post at 10:00 and the race officially was started at 19:15.

The argument started when the drivers protested against disqualification of Howdy Wilcox in his Gilmore Special and the substitution of Mauri Rose as driver.

Wilcox had been pronounced unfit physically for the grind, physicians asserting they had learned that he suffered from fainting spells.

When Rose prepared to climb into the car, a howl of protest went up from fifteen or more drivers.

Eddie Edenburn, A.A.A. official, and Eddie Rickenbacker, president of the Speedway Corporation, entered the battle.

The drivers claimed they would not take to the bricks with Rose, who never had driven the car previously in competition.

Rickenbacker told them that, regardless of their attitude, the race would start, even if the field consisted only of two racers.

Drivers and officials finally compromised, with Rose being permitted to drive. His car was placed at the end of the field at the start.

He drove a remarkable race, pulling his car from last place to fourth.
